claim: Choanoflagellates are the closest unicellular relatives of animals.
source: As the closest unicellular relatives of animals, choanoflagellates serve as useful model organisms for understanding the evolution of animal multicellularity.
evidence: This is supported by citations to established scientific literature and represents established scientific knowledge in the field.

claim: Increasing ocean oxygen levels in the Precambrian are thought to have influenced the emergence of complex multicellular life.
source: An important factor in animal evolution was the increasing ocean oxygen levels in the Precambrian, which are thought to have influenced the emergence of complex multicellular life.
evidence: This represents established scientific consensus about Precambrian conditions and animal evolution.

claim: Salpingoeca rosetta displays positive aerotaxis.
source: Using a microfluidic device that allows spatio-temporal variations in oxygen concentrations, we report the discovery that S. rosetta displays positive aerotaxis.
evidence: This is a primary finding supported by experimental data presented in the manuscript, including Figures 3 and Videos 1-2.

claim: S. rosetta exhibits logarithmic sensing of oxygen.
source: Analysis of the spatial population distributions provides evidence for logarithmic sensing of oxygen, which enhances sensing in low oxygen neighborhoods.
evidence: This is supported by experimental data analysis and mathematical modeling presented in the manuscript.

claim: Choanoflagellate aerotaxis is consistent with stochastic navigation.
source: Analysis of search strategy models on the experimental colony trajectories finds that choanoflagellate aerotaxis is consistent with stochastic navigation, the statistics of which are captured using an effective continuous version based on classical run-and-tumble chemotaxis.
evidence: This is supported by statistical analysis of trajectory data and comparison with mathematical models.

claim: Bacteria perform chemotaxis towards nutrients.
source: Bacteria do chemotaxis towards nutrients (Adler, 1969; Berg, 1993) and away from toxins (Tso and Adler, 1974).
evidence: This is supported by citations to established literature.

claim: Algae perform phototaxis towards light.
source: Algae do phototaxis towards light (Yoshimura and Kamiya, 2001; Drescher et al., 2010) and gyrotaxis along gravitational potentials (Kessler, 1985).
evidence: This is supported by citations to established literature.

claim: Aerotaxis is well-characterized in bacteria.
source: Aerotaxis, defined as oxygen-dependent migration, is well-characterized in bacteria (Taylor et al., 1999), but is poorly studied in more complex organisms.
evidence: This is supported by citation to established literature.

claim: Aerotaxis is poorly studied in complex organisms.
source: Aerotaxis, defined as oxygen-dependent migration, is well-characterized in bacteria (Taylor et al., 1999), but is poorly studied in more complex organisms.
evidence: This represents a knowledge gap in the field based on literature review.

claim: Precambrian oxygen levels played an important role in the emergence and evolution of multicellular animal life.
source: This is despite the essentiality of oxygen for all aerobic life, and the important role that Precambrian oxygen levels played in the emergence and evolution of multicellular animal life (Nursall, 1959).
evidence: This is supported by citation to established literature.

claim: Choanoflagellates are the closest relatives of animals.
source: Choanoflagellates are a class of unicellular microorganisms that are the closest relatives of the animals (Lang et al., 2002).
evidence: This is supported by citation to molecular phylogenetic evidence.

claim: The relationship between choanoflagellates and animals was first proposed by James-Clark in 1866.
source: This relationship was first proposed by James-Clark in 1866 (James-Clark, 1866), on the basis of the resemblance between choanoflagellates and the choanocytes of sponges.
evidence: This is a historical fact supported by citation.

claim: The sister relationship between choanoflagellates and animals was confirmed by molecular evidence.
source: The sister relationship between choanoflagellates and animals was further confirmed in the genomic era by molecular evidence (King et al., 2008).
evidence: This is supported by citation to genomic studies.

claim: All choanoflagellates share the same basic unicell structure consisting of a prolate cell body with a single beating flagellum surrounded by a collar of microvilli.
source: All choanoflagellates share the same basic unicell structure: a prolate cell body with a single beating flagellum that is surrounded by a collar of microvilli.
evidence: This represents established knowledge about choanoflagellate morphology.

claim: The beating of the flagellum creates a current that guides suspended prey through the collar where they can be caught and phagocytosed.
source: The beating of the flagellum creates a current in the surrounding fluid that guides suspended prey such as bacteria through the collar (Pettitt and Orme, 2002) where they can be caught and ultimately phagocytosed.
evidence: This is supported by citation to established literature on choanoflagellate feeding.

claim: The flagellar current causes the choanoflagellate cell to swim.
source: The flagellar current also has the effect of causing the choanoflagellate cell to swim.
evidence: This is an inference from the physics of flagellar beating and fluid dynamics.

claim: Salpingoeca rosetta can form colonies through incomplete cytokinesis.
source: The choanoflagellate Salpingoeca rosetta can form colonies through incomplete cytokinesis (Fairclough et al., 2010).
evidence: This is supported by citation to established literature.

claim: S. rosetta colonies have a rosette-like shape in the presence of certain bacteria.
source: In the presence of certain bacteria (Dayel et al., 2011; Levin et al., 2014), these colonies have an eponymous rosette-like shape as shown in Figure 1.
evidence: This is supported by citations and visual evidence in Figure 1.

claim: S. rosetta colony morphology is variable.
source: The colony morphology is variable, and the constituent flagella beat independently of one another (Kirkegaard et al., 2016).
evidence: This is supported by citation to previous work.

claim: The constituent flagella of S. rosetta colonies beat independently of one another.
source: The colony morphology is variable, and the constituent flagella beat independently of one another (Kirkegaard et al., 2016).
evidence: This is supported by citation to previous work.

claim: The random and independent flagellar motion argues against coordination between cells in a colony.
source: The random and independent flagellar motion argues against there being any coordination between cells in a colony, and as yet no evidence of any form of taxis for choanoflagellate colonies has been reported.
evidence: This is an inference from the observation of independent flagellar beating.

claim: No evidence of any form of taxis for choanoflagellate colonies had been reported prior to this study.
source: The random and independent flagellar motion argues against there being any coordination between cells in a colony, and as yet no evidence of any form of taxis for choanoflagellate colonies has been reported.
evidence: This represents a knowledge gap in the literature prior to this study.

claim: Cell body diameters of S. rosetta are approximately 5 µm.
source: Cell body diameters are ~5 µm.
evidence: This is a measurement reported in the figure caption.

claim: Volvocales are a group of green algae.
source: The geometry, flagella independence and lack of taxis observed in S. rosetta colonies contrast with other lineages, such as the Volvocales, a group of green algae (Goldstein, 2015).
evidence: This is established taxonomic knowledge supported by citation.

claim: Phototaxis is observable in both unicellular (Chlamydomonas) and colonial (Volvox) Volvocales species.
source: Phototaxis is clearly observable in both unicellular (Chlamydomonas) (Yoshimura and Kamiya, 2001) and colonial (Volvox) (Drescher et al., 2010) species, in order to maintain optimum light levels for photosynthesis.
evidence: This is supported by citations to established literature.

claim: Volvocalean phototaxis is deterministic.
source: Volvocalean phototaxis is deterministic, requiring precise tuning between the internal biochemical timescales and the rotation period of the organism as a whole.
evidence: This represents established knowledge about Volvocales navigation mechanisms.

claim: S. rosetta colonies rotate around an internal axis.
source: Although S. rosetta colonies also rotate around an internal axis, due to the variable colony morphology and the independent beating of the individual flagella, this rotation rate will itself be random (Kirkegaard et al., 2016), rendering a strategy similar to that of the Volvocales unlikely in S. rosetta.
evidence: This is supported by citation to previous work.

claim: The rotation rate of S. rosetta colonies is random due to variable colony morphology and independent flagellar beating.
source: Although S. rosetta colonies also rotate around an internal axis, due to the variable colony morphology and the independent beating of the individual flagella, this rotation rate will itself be random (Kirkegaard et al., 2016), rendering a strategy similar to that of the Volvocales unlikely in S. rosetta.
evidence: This is an inference from observations supported by citation.

claim: A navigation strategy similar to that of the Volvocales is unlikely in S. rosetta.
source: Although S. rosetta colonies also rotate around an internal axis, due to the variable colony morphology and the independent beating of the individual flagella, this rotation rate will itself be random (Kirkegaard et al., 2016), rendering a strategy similar to that of the Volvocales unlikely in S. rosetta.
evidence: This is an inference based on the differences in rotation characteristics.

claim: Stochastic taxis is sometimes referred to as kinesis.
source: An alternative strategy is stochastic taxis, sometimes referred to as kinesis.
evidence: This is established terminology in the field.

claim: Run-and-tumble chemotaxis of peritrichous bacteria is a classic example of stochastic taxis.
source: The classic example of stochastic taxis is the run-and-tumble chemotaxis of certain peritrichous bacteria (Berg, 1993).
evidence: This is supported by citation to established literature.

claim: Bacteria can alternate between swimming in straight lines (running) and randomly reorienting themselves (tumbling) by spinning their flagella in different directions.
source: By spinning their left-handed helical flagella in different directions, such bacteria can alternate between swimming in straight lines (running) and randomly reorienting themselves (tumbling).
evidence: This represents established knowledge about bacterial motility.

claim: Bacteria exhibit biased motion towards a chemoattractant by biasing tumbles to be less frequent when going up the gradient.
source: Through biasing tumbles to be less frequent when going up the gradient, the bacteria exhibit biased motion towards a chemoattractant without directly steering towards it (Berg, 1993).
evidence: This is supported by citation to established literature.

claim: PDMS is permeable to gases.
source: Since PDMS, the most commonly used material for microfluidic chambers, is permeable to gases, gas channels can be introduced in the devices to allow gaseous species to diffuse into the fluid.
evidence: This is established knowledge about material properties.

claim: An oxygen gradient can be created using a source channel flowing with normal air and a sink channel flowing with pure nitrogen.
source: For example, an oxygen gradient can be created using a source channel flowing with normal air and a sink channel flowing with pure nitrogen.
evidence: This is a methodological approach described in the manuscript.

claim: The microfluidic device used is a modified version of that used by Adler, et al.
source: Our device, shown schematically in Figure 2, is a modified version of that used by Adler, et al. (Adler et al., 2012).
evidence: This is supported by citation and description of the device.

claim: The thickness of the microfluidic channels is approximately 115 µm.
source: Thickness of the channels are ≈115 µm.
evidence: This is a measurement reported in the figure caption.

claim: Experiments were carried out immediately after plasma etching because the permeability of gases slowly decreases thereafter.
source: Experiments were carried out immediately after plasma etching as the permeability of gases slowly decreases thereafter.
evidence: This is a methodological consideration based on material properties.

claim: S. rosetta colonies accumulate at the oxygen-rich side and away from the oxygen-poor side.
source: Our main experimental result, shown in Figure 3a,b, is the observation that S. rosetta colonies accumulate at the oxygen-rich side and away from the oxygen-poor side, i.e. that they are aerotactic.
evidence: This is the primary experimental finding supported by visual data in Figure 3.

claim: The unicellular fast swimmer form of S. rosetta also exhibits aerotaxis.
source: We also found aerotaxis in the unicellular fast swimmer form (Dayel et al., 2011) of S. rosetta, showing that this is not an exclusive phenomenon to colonies.
evidence: This is an experimental observation reported in the manuscript.

claim: Aerotaxis is not an exclusive phenomenon to S. rosetta colonies.
source: We also found aerotaxis in the unicellular fast swimmer form (Dayel et al., 2011) of S. rosetta, showing that this is not an exclusive phenomenon to colonies.
evidence: This is an inference from the observation that both unicellular and colonial forms exhibit aerotaxis.

claim: When there is oxygen in both gas channels, the density reaches an approximately uniform distribution within the time frame of the experiment.
source: When there is oxygen in both gas channels, we observe that the density reaches an approximately uniform distribution within the time frame of the experiment.
evidence: This is an experimental observation from the density evolution data.

claim: When nitrogen flows in both channels, colonies accumulate in the middle of the chamber where there is still some residual oxygen.
source: For periods in which nitrogen flows in both channels, this is not the case. Under these experimental conditions, the colonies accumulate in the middle of the chamber, where there is still some residual oxygen, as further shown in Video 2.
evidence: This is supported by experimental data shown in Video 2.

claim: Colony accumulation does not depend on the presence of a nearby surface.
source: The fact that in this nitrogen-only configuration the colonies accumulate mid-chamber shows that accumulation does not depend on the presence of a nearby surface.
evidence: This is an inference from the observation of mid-chamber accumulation.

claim: Colonies stay in the middle of chamber even after 90 min with only nitrogen flowing.
source: With only nitrogen flowing, eventually there will be no oxygen gradient. Nonetheless, we observed the colonies to stay in the middle of chamber even after 90 min (see Figure 3—figure supplement 1).
evidence: This is an experimental observation supported by supplementary figure data.

claim: After 90 min with only nitrogen flowing, the highest oxygen levels are estimated to be less than approximately 0.2%.
source: At that time, the highest oxygen levels are estimated by the diffusion equation to be less than ~0.2%.
evidence: This is a calculation based on the diffusion equation model.

claim: The contrasting behaviour between oxygen-only and nitrogen-only configurations suggests an asymmetry or non-linearity in the aerotactic response.
source: This contrasting behaviour between the oxygen-only and nitrogen-only configurations suggests an asymmetry or non-linearity in the aerotactic response.
evidence: This is an inference from the experimental observations.

claim: If the response to oxygen concentration had been linear, the observation of the density band in the nitrogen-only section would imply similar density bands at the chamber edges in the oxygen-only section.
source: If the response to oxygen concentration had been linear, the observation of the density band in the nitrogen-only section would imply similar density bands at the chamber edges in the oxygen-only section, which is not observed.
evidence: This is a logical inference about what would be expected under linear sensing.

claim: The hypothesis of logarithmic sensing can quantitatively explain the experiments.
source: This is also known as logarithmic sensing, and we will confirm in the modelling section that this hypothesis can quantitatively explain the experiments.
evidence: This is supported by the modeling results presented later in the manuscript.

claim: Strategies of taxis can be categorized into two main classes: deterministic and stochastic.
source: Strategies of taxis can be categorized into two main classes: deterministic and stochastic.
evidence: This is established knowledge in the field of taxis research.

claim: In a deterministic strategy, the organism directly steers towards the attractant.
source: A deterministic strategy, then, is one in which the organism directly steers towards the attractant, such as seen in sperm cells that modulate their flagellar beat to adjust directly the curvature and torsion of its swimming path in the gradient direction (Friedrich and Jülicher, 2007; Jikeli et al., 2015).
evidence: This is supported by citations to established literature.

claim: In a stochastic strategy, modulation of the frequency of random reorientations biases motion in the gradient direction without directly steering towards it.
source: Contrasting is a stochastic strategy such as bacterial run-and-tumble locomotion (Berg, 1993), where modulation of the frequency of random reorientations biases the motion in the gradient direction without directly steering towards it.
evidence: This is supported by citation to established literature.

claim: The ensemble average swimming speed does not show an increase after a gas channel swap.
source: For most times, the component velocities average to zero, but after a gas channel swap the y-component peaks. The ensemble average swimming speed in these sections, however, does not show an increase, suggesting that a velocity modulation is not the method of taxis.
evidence: This is an observation from the velocity analysis shown in Figure 4.

claim: Velocity modulation is not the method of taxis in S. rosetta.
source: The ensemble average swimming speed in these sections, however, does not show an increase, suggesting that a velocity modulation is not the method of taxis.
evidence: This is an inference from the velocity data analysis.

claim: Swimming speed shows a very small (~3%) change when going up the gradient.
source: The plot shows a very small (~3%) change in swimming speed going up the gradient.
evidence: This is a quantitative measurement from the data analysis shown in Figure 4 inset.

claim: To obtain a drift velocity ~1/3 of the swimming velocity through velocity modulation would require γ = 2/3 for a two-dimensional swimmer and γ = 1 in three dimensions.
source: To obtain a drift velocity ~1/3 of the swimming velocity, as we find for S. rosetta in the following section, the velocity modulation would have to be γ= 2/3 for a two-dimensional swimmer and γ = 1 in three dimensions, much larger than the ~3% observed.
evidence: This is a calculation based on theoretical models of velocity-biased taxis.

claim: The primary mechanism of aerotaxis in S. rosetta is not a modulation of swimming speed.
source: We conclude that the primary mechanism of aerotaxis in S. rosetta is therefore not a modulation of swimming speed.
evidence: This is a conclusion drawn from the velocity analysis data.

claim: S. rosetta colonies swim along noisy helical paths.
source: S. rosetta colonies swim along noisy helical paths, and each colony displays distinct helix parameters (Kirkegaard et al., 2016).
evidence: This is supported by citation to previous work.

claim: Each S. rosetta colony displays distinct helix parameters.
source: S. rosetta colonies swim along noisy helical paths, and each colony displays distinct helix parameters (Kirkegaard et al., 2016).
evidence: This is supported by citation to previous work.

claim: The angular distribution during swaps favors the up-direction θ=π/2.
source: This distribution favors the up-direction θ=π/2.
evidence: This is an observation from the angular distribution data shown in Figure 5a.

claim: The distribution of reorientations is centred on zero.
source: The distribution is centred on zero, revealing that the colonies do as many turns in the wrong direction as in the correct direction.
evidence: This is an observation from the reorientation distribution data shown in Figure 5b.

claim: The colonies do as many turns in the wrong direction as in the correct direction.
source: The distribution is centred on zero, revealing that the colonies do as many turns in the wrong direction as in the correct direction.
evidence: This is an inference from the reorientation distribution data.

claim: The colonies navigate by a stochastic strategy.
source: This indicates that the colonies navigate by a stochastic strategy.
evidence: This is a conclusion drawn from the reorientation distribution analysis.

claim: The Keller-Segel model has broad applicability for taxis.
source: We study the spatio-temporal evolution of the choanoflagellate colony population within the observation chamber with the Keller-Segel model (Keller and Segel, 1971), which has broad applicability for taxis (Tindall et al., 2008).
evidence: This is supported by citations to established literature.

claim: The concentration field is approximately constant along the x-direction.
source: To a very good approximation the concentration field is constant along the x-direction.
evidence: This is an observation from the numerical simulation results shown in Figure 6b.

claim: A linear response functional can reach unrealistic drift velocities if oxygen gradients are large.
source: Such a response can, however, reach unrealistic drift velocities, i.e. higher than the swimming velocity, if the oxygen gradients are large.
evidence: This is a known limitation of the linear response model.

claim: Most of the behaviour in Figure 3c can be explained by the model with response functional V[c]=v_drift tanh(α|∇c|)∇c/|∇c|.
source: Most of the behaviour of Figure 3c can be explained by this model (See Figure 3—figure supplement 1), but not the section where nitrogen is flowing in both side channels.
evidence: This is supported by comparison of model results with experimental data in the supplement.

claim: The model with linear gradient sensing cannot explain the section where nitrogen is flowing in both side channels.
source: Most of the behaviour of Figure 3c can be explained by this model (See Figure 3—figure supplement 1), but not the section where nitrogen is flowing in both side channels.
evidence: This is an observation from comparing model predictions with experimental data.

claim: The Keller-Segel equation with log-sensing can explain all sections of the experiment.
source: The Keller-Segel equation with log-sensing is able to explain all sections of the experiment, as demonstrated in Figure 3d.
evidence: This is supported by the model fit shown in Figure 3d.

claim: Translational diffusion due to thermal noise is orders of magnitude smaller than active diffusion.
source: We furthermore ignore translational diffusion due to thermal noise, since this contribution is orders of magnitude smaller than that of active diffusion.
evidence: This is based on established knowledge about the relative magnitudes of thermal and active diffusion for microorganisms.

claim: Both deterministic and stochastic models can describe the angle distribution data in Figure 5a well.
source: Both models are able to describe the data in Figure 5a well, with the deterministic model (purple) fitting the down-gradient swimming best, and the stochastic model (green) fitting the up-gradient swimming best.
evidence: This is supported by the model fits shown in Figure 5a.

claim: The deterministic model does not provide a satisfactory fit to the reorientation data.
source: We see clearly that the deterministic model does not provide a satisfactory fit to the data.
evidence: This is an observation from comparing the deterministic model prediction with the data in Figure 5b.

claim: The colonies navigate by a stochastic strategy based on the angle statistics analysis.
source: We thus conclude that the colonies navigate by a stochastic strategy, and that the ensemble angle statistics can be captured by this simple model.
evidence: This is a conclusion drawn from the statistical analysis of trajectory data.

claim: The ensemble angle statistics can be captured by the stochastic model.
source: We thus conclude that the colonies navigate by a stochastic strategy, and that the ensemble angle statistics can be captured by this simple model.
evidence: This is supported by the model fits to the experimental data.

claim: Colonies of S. rosetta can navigate along gradients of oxygen.
source: We have shown that colonies of S. rosetta can navigate along gradients of oxygen, thus exhibiting positive aerotaxis.
evidence: This is the main conclusion summarizing the experimental findings.

claim: The cells navigate along relative oxygen gradients.
source: The cells navigate along relative oxygen gradients and the navigation strategy is stochastic in nature, achieved by modulating not speed but direction of swimming.
evidence: This is a conclusion from the modeling and data analysis.

claim: The navigation strategy is stochastic in nature.
source: The cells navigate along relative oxygen gradients and the navigation strategy is stochastic in nature, achieved by modulating not speed but direction of swimming.
evidence: This is a conclusion from the statistical analysis of trajectories.

claim: Aerotaxis is achieved by modulating direction of swimming, not speed.
source: The cells navigate along relative oxygen gradients and the navigation strategy is stochastic in nature, achieved by modulating not speed but direction of swimming.
evidence: This is a conclusion from the velocity and angle analysis.

claim: In animals, oxygen concentrations can be sensed by the hypoxia-inducible factor (HIF) transcription factor pathway.
source: In animals, oxygen concentrations can be sensed by the highly-conserved hypoxia-inducible factor (HIF) transcription factor pathway (Loenarz et al., 2011; Kaelin and Ratcliffe, 2008; Rytkönen et al., 2011).
evidence: This is supported by citations to established literature.

claim: At normal oxygen levels, prolyl-hydroxylase (PHD) enzyme activity labels HIF protein complexes for degradation.
source: At normal oxygen levels, the activity of specific prolyl-hydroxylase (PHD) enzymes labels the HIF protein complexes for degradation.
evidence: This is established knowledge about the HIF pathway.

claim: At low oxygen levels, PHD activity is inhibited, leading to elevated HIF levels.
source: At low oxygen levels, however, PHD activity is inhibited, leading to elevated HIF levels.
evidence: This is established knowledge about the HIF pathway.

claim: HIF up-regulates expression of genes involved in hypoxia response for survival in low-oxygen conditions.
source: The transcription factor activity of HIF up-regulates expression of genes involved in hypoxia response (e.g. glycolysis enzymes) for survival in low-oxygen conditions (Greer et al., 2012).
evidence: This is supported by citation to established literature.

claim: The genes involved in HIF signalling are widespread in metazoans.
source: The genes involved in HIF signalling are widespread in metazoans, with evidence suggesting that some components of this pathway are descended from prokaryotic ancestors (Scotti et al., 2014).
evidence: This is supported by citation to established literature.

claim: Some components of the HIF pathway are descended from prokaryotic ancestors.
source: The genes involved in HIF signalling are widespread in metazoans, with evidence suggesting that some components of this pathway are descended from prokaryotic ancestors (Scotti et al., 2014).
evidence: This is supported by citation to established literature.

claim: Exposing S. rosetta cultures to DMOG had no observable effect on aerotaxis.
source: Preliminary experiments involving exposing S. rosetta cultures to DMOG (an inhibitor of the prolyl-hydroxylase step in the HIF pathway [Fong and Takeda, 2008]) had no observable effect on aerotaxis within our experimental system (data not shown).
evidence: This is an experimental observation reported in the manuscript.

claim: Choanoflagellates lack some important components of the HIF pathway.
source: This is perhaps unsurprising, given that choanoflagellates lack some important components of the HIF pathway (Rytkönen et al., 2011).
evidence: This is supported by citation to established literature.

claim: The aerotactic response observed is acute, within a timeframe on the order of seconds to minutes.
source: Additionally, the aerotactic response observed here is acute, within a timeframe on the order of seconds to minutes, rather than the being a longer-term response to lowered oxygen levels by modulation of gene expression.
evidence: This is an observation from the experimental timescales.

claim: In certain aerotactic bacteria, oxygen concentrations are measured indirectly via energy-sensing.
source: In certain aerotactic bacteria, it is known that oxygen concentrations are measured indirectly via energy-sensing, which can then influence the rotation of the bacterial flagella between running and tumbling (Taylor et al., 1999).
evidence: This is supported by citation to established literature.

claim: An analogous mechanism to bacterial energy-sensing may be at play in choanoflagellates.
source: An analogous mechanism may be at play in choanoflagellates, possibly via reactive oxygen species (Cash et al., 2007) and oxygen-sensitive ion channels (Lahiri et al., 2006; Ward, 2008) modulating the beating rate of the flagella of each S. rosetta cell.
evidence: This is speculation about possible mechanisms supported by citations to relevant literature.

claim: Oxygen is implicated as having an important influence on animal evolution.
source: Oxygen is implicated as having an important influence on animal evolution (Nursall, 1959; Lenton et al., 2014), with some hypotheses that the emergence of complex animal ecosystems (Sperling et al., 2013) were only triggered when oxygen levels rose above certain thresholds.
evidence: This is supported by citations to established literature.

claim: Sponges were recently shown to have very low oxygen requirements.
source: Sponges, believed to be the most basal animal group, were recently shown to have very low oxygen requirements, disputing the importance of oxygen in early animal evolution (Mills et al., 2014).
evidence: This is supported by citation to recent literature.

claim: The common ancestor from which choanoflagellates and animals evolved may have been aerotactic.
source: Our results raise the possibility that the common ancestor from which choanoflagellates and animals evolved was aerotactic, and that oxygen sensing and responding have thus been under strong selection throughout the holozoans.
evidence: This is speculation based on the experimental findings.

claim: If the ancestors of animals and choanoflagellates were strongly aerotactic, this would be indicative of the importance of oxygen as a resource during the Precambrian.
source: If the ancestors of animals and choanoflagellates were strongly aerotactic, this would be indicative of the importance of oxygen as a resource during the Precambrian (Lyons et al., 2014).
evidence: This is a speculative inference about evolutionary implications.

claim: It could be the case that choanoflagellates themselves have evolved aerotaxis after the split from the animal stem lineage.
source: Equally, it could be the case that choanoflagellates themselves have evolved aerotaxis after the split from the animal stem lineage.
evidence: This is an alternative speculation about the evolutionary origin of aerotaxis.

claim: Both the unicellular and colonial morphotypes of S. rosetta can perform efficient aerotaxis.
source: Our experimental results show that both the unicellular and colonial morphotypes of S. rosetta can perform efficient aerotaxis and navigation in general, despite lacking coordination between the constituent cells of the colony (Kirkegaard et al., 2016).
evidence: This is a conclusion from the experimental observations.

claim: An evolutionary transition to multicellularity resembling the unicellular-to-colonial transition in S. rosetta would not require additional cell-cell communication mechanisms to coordinate navigation.
source: Therefore, an evolutionary transition to a multicellularity resembling the unicellular-to-colonial transition in S. rosetta (Dayel et al., 2011) would not require additional cell-cell communication mechanisms to coordinate navigation.
evidence: This is an inference from the observation that both forms can navigate without coordination.

claim: The stochastic navigation strategy works equally well for both single cells and colonies formed from multiple units of the same cells.
source: This is a particular feature of the stochastic navigation strategy, which works equally well for both single cells and colonies formed from multiple units of the same cells.
evidence: This is an inference about the properties of stochastic navigation.

claim: Logarithmic sensing allows sensing of and reacting to gradients in very low concentration environments while still being able to effectively navigate along large gradients.
source: Logarithmic sensing is a key attribute for survival: it allows sensing of and reacting to gradients in very low concentration environments, while still being able to effectively navigate along large gradients.
evidence: This is an inference about the functional advantages of logarithmic sensing.

claim: Logarithmic sensing has been experimentally observed in bacteria.
source: Logarithmic sensing has also been experimentally observed for other species, e.g. bacteria (Mesibov et al., 1973; Kalinin et al., 2009).
evidence: This is supported by citations to established literature.

claim: Weber's law states that the magnitude of just-noticeable differences of a stimulus is proportional to the stimulus magnitude itself.
source: It is known as Weber's law (Ross, 1996), which states that the magnitude of just-noticeable differences of a stimuli is proportional to the stimuli magnitude itself.
evidence: This is established knowledge in psychophysics supported by citation.

claim: The Weber-Fechner law states that stimulus magnitude grows logarithmically with the actual signal.
source: This is closely related to the Weber-Fechner law, stating that stimuli magnitude grows logarithmically with the actual signal, which we have found to be in agreement with the experimental observation of S. rosetta aerotaxis.
evidence: This is established knowledge supported by the experimental findings.

claim: The error on any concentration gradient measurement increases with the local absolute concentration due to thermal fluctuations.
source: Because of thermal fluctuations, the error on any concentration gradient measurement increases with the local absolute concentration (Berg and Purcell, 1977; Endres and Wingreen, 2008), and thus it immediately follows that the limit of just-noticeable gradients must decrease with absolute concentration.
evidence: This is supported by citations to theoretical work on sensing limits.

claim: The fitting of the Keller-Segel model to the population data was optimal for relative gradient sensing.
source: The fitting of the Keller-Segel model to the population data were optimal precisely for relative gradient sensing.
evidence: This is a result from the model fitting analysis.

claim: Weber's law and logarithmic sensing occur in choanoflagellates, at least to a good approximation.
source: This implies that Weber's law and logarithmic sensing, at least to a good approximation, is occurring in chaonoflagellates.
evidence: This is a conclusion from the model fitting results.

claim: The master for microfluidic devices was produced by spinning SU8-2075 at 1200 rpm to a thickness of approximately 115 µm.
source: The master was produced by spinning SU8-2075 (MicroChem, USA) at 1200 rpm to a thickness of ~115 µm.
evidence: This is a description of the fabrication methods.

claim: Chambers were cast in PDMS and plasma etched to glass slides.
source: Chambers were cast in PDMS, Sylgard 184 (Dow Corning, USA), and plasma etched to the glass slides.
